claims.text: Adding approximately 1 wt% silver nanoparticles to W–Cu precursor powders before sintering will increase the composite's thermal conductivity.
Silver nanoparticle addition will improve interfacial bonding between the tungsten and copper phases.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding will reduce thermal resistance at phase boundaries.
The silver addition will not compromise mechanical durability.
The silver addition will not compromise irradiation resistance.
A conventional W–Cu composite can be made by mixing, compacting, and sintering tungsten and copper powders at around 1000 °C in a reducing atmosphere.
The proposed intervention is addition of approximately 1 wt% silver nanoparticles to the precursor powder mixture before sintering.
Silver nanoparticles will act as conductive bridges at W–Cu interfaces.
Conductive bridges at W–Cu interfaces will improve thermal pathways across phase boundaries.
Silver has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Silver can form coherent interfacial bonds with both tungsten and copper.
Silver nanoparticles will occupy and modify defect-rich W–Cu interfacial regions.
Modification of the interfaces by silver nanoparticles will reduce phonon scattering and interfacial thermal resistance.
The interface modification will not introduce defects that undermine mechanical strength or radiation tolerance.
The silver-doped composite will retain mechanical durability similar to that of an otherwise comparable undoped W–Cu composite.
The silver-doped composite will retain irradiation resistance similar to that of an otherwise comparable undoped W–Cu composite.
The predicted outcome is intended to hold for typical W–Cu ratios and processing conditions used in high-heat-flux and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Changes in phase distribution or processing parameters may alter the predicted outcome.
Silver nanoparticle agglomeration or irradiation-induced interfacial reactions could modify the expected behavior.
